questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: In systems languages (`C`, `C++`, `Rust`), how do Stack memory and Heap memory differ fundamentally?

options.text: Stack memory grows unbounded across gigabytes safely
Heap memory is strictly faster than CPU registers
Stack uses fast LIFO frame allocation scoped to function calls; Heap enables dynamic variable-lifetime allocation requiring explicit deallocation or RAII/ownership
Heap allocations never require pointers or references

questions.explanation: Understanding stack frames vs heap allocation explains lifetimes, buffer overflows, leaks, and Rust/C++ ownership idioms.

questions.prompt: What compile-time guarantee makes Rust eliminate data races and dangling pointers without a garbage collector?

options.text: Disabling multithreading across OS cores
Ownership and the Borrow Checker: each value has one owner and allows either multiple immutable (`&T`) or one single mutable (`&mut T`) borrow at a time
Runtime pause-the-world tracing garbage collection every 10ms
Automatic conversion of every integer into a heap object

questions.explanation: Rust's aliasing XOR mutability rules enforce memory safety and data-race freedom statically at compile time.

Using raw C-style `malloc()` without `free()`
Suppressing exceptions with `catch (...) {}`

questions.sectionTitle: Section A: Multiple Choice Questions & Fundamentals
questions.prompt: In JVM / .NET (`Java`, `C#`), why is comparing two object/string contents with `==` often hazardous compared to `.Equals()` / `.equals()`?

options.text: Strings are value structs on the CPU stack in Java
`==` fails compilation in C#
`==` on reference types checks whether two pointers reference the same heap identity rather than comparing content equality
`.equals()` only checks memory addresses

questions.explanation: Java String equality requires `.equals()` to compare characters reliably (as non-interned heap instances hold different references).

questions.prompt: Which errors occur from unsafe manual pointer/buffer manipulation in C?

options.text: Buffer overflow writing past allocated array bounds (`strcpy` vs bounded `snprintf`)
Use-after-free accessing heap pointers already passed to `free()`
Null pointer dereference reading memory address `0x0`
Automatic bounds expansion allocating RAM cleanly at runtime

questions.prompt: In C# / .NET asynchronous programming, why should `async void` methods generally be avoided except for top-level UI event handlers?

`async void` executes code twice
`Task` is deprecated in .NET 8+

questions.prompt: What dangerous undefined behavior occurs in C if a function returns the address of a local array (`int buf[10]; return buf;`)?

options.text: The array values are frozen permanently as read-only constants
Compilers convert local arrays to global static variables implicitly
The local array resides on the function's stack frame, which is popped on return—leaving a dangling pointer to overwritten memory
C automatically promotes stack arrays to garbage-collected heap memory

questions.explanation: Never return pointers to stack-local storage; pass caller-owned output buffers (`out_len`) or heap-allocate with clear ownership.

questions.prompt: In Go, spinning up 10,000 goroutines reading/writing an unguarded `map[string]int` panics at runtime (`fatal error: concurrent map read and map write`). Fix?

options.text: Protect map access with `sync.RWMutex`, use `sync.Map`, or funnel writes through a dedicated owner goroutine via channels
Cast the map to `interface{}`
Wrap calls in `defer recover()` assuming writes didn't corrupt memory
Use global slice indexing without locks

questions.explanation: Built-in Go maps are intentionally non-thread-safe for zero-overhead single-goroutine speed and must be synchronized explicitly.

questions.prompt: Look at this Rust snippet: `let s1 = String::from("twin"); let s2 = s1; println!("{}", s1);`. Why does `rustc` reject compilation?

options.text: `println!` forbids printing Strings
Rust Strings cannot exceed 4 characters
`let` bindings are write-only
`s1` was moved into `s2` transferring heap ownership; using `s1` afterward would cause double-free/use-after-free unless borrowed (`&s1`) or `.clone()`ed
